claims.text: Inhibiting precursor mobility during low-temperature reduction promotes stochastic reduction behavior.
Immobilization causes all metal species to reduce nearly simultaneously.
Inhibiting precursor mobility favors formation of single-phase high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles rather than phase-separated products.
The initial material is a uniformly mixed precipitate of five noble-metal ion precursors.
The five precursor elements can be Pt, Ir, Os, Rh, and Ru, supplied through cationic and anionic aqueous precursor solutions.
Rapid mixing and immediate precipitation inhibit precursor mobility.
The relevant synthesis regime is low-temperature and solution-based.
At the stated low temperatures, thermal energy is insufficient for conventional entropy-driven stabilization.
In situ X-ray powder diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy can follow nanoparticle crystallization and reduction of the constituent elements.
Reduced precursor mobility prevents sequential or spatially localized reduction that would otherwise cause elemental segregation.
Stochastic co-reduction favors a homogeneous distribution of metal atoms within a single-phase structure.
Mobility-inhibiting conditions will produce nanoparticles with a single-phase alloy structure.
Mobility-inhibiting conditions will produce a uniform elemental distribution detectable by XRD and XAS.
Unrestrained precursor mobility will lead to phase separation or elemental segregation.
High-mobility baseline syntheses undergo sequential reduction or localized clustering that results in phase separation.
The hypothesis primarily applies to low-temperature syntheses of noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The hypothesis may not apply under high-temperature, entropy-dominated synthesis conditions.
The hypothesis may not apply to systems with substantially different precursor chemistries.
The required degree of mobility inhibition and the effects of ligand environment on reduction kinetics remain unquantified.

Indistinguishable single-phase, compositionally homogeneous products from the mobility-inhibited condition and its otherwise identical control would falsify the proposed causal role of mobility inhibition.
